title: Mammal-conserved human DNA far from mapped accessible chromatin is under strong selection in 76,215 genomes mainly within 1 kb of exons, and new chromatin catalogues add little of it
abstract:
Human non-coding DNA that 241 mammals conserve but that no chromatin map marks as accessible is under natural selection in present-day humans; within 1 kb of an exon this selection is as strong as in conserved DNA inside accessible chromatin, but further away it is about 0.4 times as strong. This matters because maps of accessible chromatin are the main guide to regulatory DNA, and a common view is that conserved DNA outside them is regulatory DNA active in cell types not yet sampled.

We marked 78.3 million autosomal non-coding bases as constrained (phyloP of 2.27 or more in the Zoonomia alignment; phyloP is a per-base conservation score). Accessible chromatin is DNA that nucleosomes do not cover. Of the constrained bases, 47.3% are in DNase I hypersensitive sites (DHSs) of 733 biosamples, 13.1% more in ENCODE v4 or single-cell CATlas elements (222 adult and fetal cell types), 18.8% within 200 bases of these, and 20.9% further away ('dark'). DNA that the two other catalogues add more than 200 bases from any DHS is 2.0-2.5% constrained, close to DNA in no DHS (2.0%); fetal neural samples are an exception.

In 76,215 genomes (gnomAD v4.1) we used a selection index: the depletion of alleles at frequency 1e-3 to 0.05 relative to alleles below 1e-4 at the same bases, which a uniformly lower mutation rate does not change. Outside transposons and segmental duplications, the index is 0.29 (95% CI 0.19-0.39) for dark constrained intronic bases within 1 kb of an exon, the same as in DHSs (0.29), but 0.08 (0.04-0.12) for dark constrained bases further away, against 0.22 in DHSs; the contrast holds at equal phyloP and against neutral bases in the same windows. Dark bases in exons of non-canonical isoforms (nonsense-mediated decay, retained intron) give 0.52. Deep dark selection is detectable mainly in elements of 20 or more bases. Near exons, dark constrained bases are 1.7-2.2 times as often in RNA-binding-protein sites (eCLIP). VISTA elements whose constrained bases were at most 10% accessible were active enhancers in mouse embryos in 4 of 39 cases, against 59% when more than 75% were accessible.

Limits: the index has a non-selective dependence on phyloP, so absolute values are less certain than comparisons at equal phyloP; up to a third or more of dark constrained bases can be phyloP false positives; the 200-base flank is a choice; eCLIP covers two cell lines. We give 32,186 dark elements and testable predictions.

display.caption: A: share of constrained bases (phyloP 2.27 or more) in accessible DNA, by the number of the 733 biosamples in which the DNA is in a DHS. Diamonds: DNA that ENCODE v4 cCREs and CATlas add outside the DHS index, within 200 bp of a DHS (orange) or more than 200 bp from any DHS (red). Dashed line: genome average. Dotted line: DNA in no DHS. B: share of bases inside a DHS as biosamples are added (solid: exact rarefaction; dashed: Chao 2014 extrapolation; triangles: Chao2 lower-bound estimate).

gnomAD v4.1 (76,215 genomes), non-CpG bases outside transposons, segmental duplications and simple repeats; 95% bootstrap intervals over windows. A: depletion of alleles by frequency class; depletion that grows with frequency is the signature of purifying selection. B: selection index of constrained bases in exons of non-canonical isoforms, in introns by distance to the nearest exon of any isoform, and in intergenic DNA, for DHS, flank and dark DNA; grey band: held-out neutral bases. C: selection index by phyloP class.

A: VISTA in vivo enhancer rate in mouse embryos against the share of an element's constrained bases that is accessible (elements with 50 or more constrained bases; Wilson 95% intervals). B: eCLIP peak rate of constrained intronic bases divided by that of unconstrained intronic bases, by distance to the nearest exon.
